title: Inpatient hyperglycaemia and perioperative glucose management
subject: endocrinology
summary: Treat persistent glucose of 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L) or more with scheduled insulin (basal plus prandial plus correction if eating, basal plus correction if not), aiming for 100 to 180 mg/dL on wards and 140 to 180 mg/dL in ICU, avoid sliding scale alone, and match insulin to steroids and surgery.

sections.title: Assess on admission
items: Hospital hyperglycaemia: any glucose above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Check HbA1c if none in the past 3 months; HbA1c 6.5% or more suggests diabetes predating admission.
Record diabetes type (type 1 must always have basal insulin), home drugs and doses, nutrition route (eating, nil by mouth, enteral, parenteral), steroid use, renal function and hypoglycaemia risk.
Point-of-care glucose before meals if eating; every 4 to 6 hours if not eating or on continuous feeds; every 30 minutes to 2 hours on IV insulin. Confirm unexpected readings in the lab.

sections.title: Targets and choice of regimen
items: Start or intensify insulin for persistent glucose of 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) or more (two readings within 24 hours).

Targets: ward (non-critical) 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6 to 10.0 mmol/L); ICU 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10.0 mmol/L), with 110 to 140 mg/dL only for selected patients (for example cardiac surgery) if achievable without hypoglycaemia.
ICU: continuous IV insulin infusion using a validated written or computerised protocol.
Eating adequately: basal plus prandial plus correction insulin. Poor or no oral intake: basal insulin plus correction insulin.

No prior diabetes, mild hyperglycaemia: correction insulin alone is acceptable at first; add scheduled insulin if 2 or more readings in 24 hours are 180 mg/dL or more. Diabetes with confirmed admission glucose 180 mg/dL or more: start scheduled insulin.

Correction-only insulin (sliding scale) as the sole regimen is discouraged, and is contraindicated in type 1 diabetes. Premixed insulins (70/30, 50/50) are not routinely recommended in hospital because of more hypoglycaemia.

sections.title: Starting doses (non-ICU)
items: Insulin-naive: total daily dose (TDD) 0.3 to 0.6 units/kg/day by weight and insulin sensitivity; use the lower end for older adults, CKD and poor intake.

Give half the TDD as basal (glargine once daily or NPH twice daily) and half as prandial rapid-acting or regular insulin split across three meals; hold prandial doses if a meal is missed. If not eating, give the basal half plus correction.
Already on insulin: start at about 80% of the home dose, adjusted for intake and illness. Basal-heavy home regimens (basal 0.6 to 1.0 units/kg/day or more) may need a 10 to 20% basal reduction.
From an IV infusion: estimate TDD from the stable rate over the last 6 to 8 hours extrapolated to 24 hours and use about 60% of it. Give SC basal 2 hours before stopping the infusion.

Correction insulin before meals (or every 4 to 6 hours if not eating), starting at 140 to 150 mg/dL (7.8 to 8.3 mmol/L), with a low, medium or high scale for TDD below 40, 40 to 80, or above 80 units/day.
Human insulins (NPH plus regular) give similar control to analogues where analogues are unaffordable, with somewhat more hypoglycaemia. Titrate doses daily.

sections.title: Non-insulin drugs in hospital
items: Hold metformin when oral intake cannot be maintained, with AKI or risk of it, and on the day of surgery or procedures.

SGLT2 inhibitors are not for inpatient glucose control: stop in severe illness, ketonaemia, prolonged fasting and surgery. They may be started or continued for heart failure once stable, with no contraindication.
Hold GLP-1 RAs in acutely ill patients. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia when intake is unreliable and are usually withheld.

Type 2 diabetes with mild hyperglycaemia (admission glucose below 180 to 200 mg/dL, HbA1c below 7.5%): a DPP-4 inhibitor plus correction insulin is an option. Avoid saxagliptin and alogliptin in heart failure.

sections.title: Glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia
items: Morning prednisolone raises glucose from midday into the evening with near-normal fasting values: check pre-lunch and pre-dinner glucose, not only fasting.

No known diabetes: if glucose is above 216 mg/dL (12 mmol/L) on 2 occasions in 24 hours, test 4 times a day and start treatment (JBDS). Target 108 to 180 mg/dL (6 to 10 mmol/L), 108 to 216 mg/dL (6 to 12 mmol/L) acceptable.

Once-daily morning steroid: morning NPH insulin given with the steroid, starting 10 units and increasing by 10 to 20% daily to target (NPH-based or basal-bolus regimens are equally acceptable). Mild cases: gliclazide 40 mg each morning, titrated daily to a maximum of 240 mg.
Dexamethasone or multiple daily doses: long-acting basal insulin is usually needed; high doses often need 40 to 60% more prandial and correction insulin.
Reduce insulin or sulfonylurea doses in step with the steroid taper to avoid hypoglycaemia.

sections.title: Perioperative
items: Elective surgery: aim for HbA1c below 8% (64 mmol/mol) within 3 months, but do not delay necessary surgery on HbA1c alone. Keep glucose 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6 to 10.0 mmol/L) before, during and after surgery.
Night before: give 75 to 80% of the usual basal analogue dose or half the usual NPH dose (individualise in type 1 diabetes, never omit basal). Monitor glucose every 2 to 4 hours while nil by mouth.
Hold metformin and other oral agents on the day of surgery. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors 3 days before surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin); after emergency surgery watch for euglycaemic DKA.
GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide: individualise; consider a 24-hour liquid diet before the procedure or full-stomach precautions if there are GI symptoms.

Insulin is the only recommended glucose-lowering drug perioperatively; use IV insulin for prolonged fasting, major surgery or poorly controlled type 1 diabetes. CGM should not be used alone during surgery.

sections.title: Enteral and parenteral nutrition
items: Continuous tube feeds: continue basal insulin and cover the feed with about 1 unit of insulin per 10 to 15 g carbohydrate, as regular insulin every 6 hours or rapid-acting every 4 hours (NPH every 8 to 12 hours is an alternative).
Parenteral nutrition: add regular insulin to the bag, starting at 1 unit per 10 g dextrose, adjusted daily. If feeds stop unexpectedly, give IV dextrose to cover insulin already given.
Type 1 diabetes must continue basal insulin even when feeds are stopped.

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia safety and discharge
items: Use a nurse-initiated hypoglycaemia protocol for glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) and review the regimen after any such value; a fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL predicts next-day hypoglycaemia (reduce basal).
Triggers: reduced intake, vomiting, stopped feeds or dextrose, steroid taper, CKD, sepsis, prandial insulin given without a meal.
Discharge: reconcile home drugs with the admission HbA1c, teach insulin technique and glucose monitoring if new, and arrange timely follow-up.

drugs.name: Insulin glargine (basal)
drugs.dose: About half the TDD (TDD 0.3 to 0.6 units/kg/day) SC once daily
drugs.notes: Continue in type 1 diabetes even if nil by mouth. Reduce if fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL.

drugs.name: NPH (isophane) insulin
drugs.dose: Basal: half the TDD split twice daily. Steroid cover: 10 units SC each morning with prednisolone, increased by 10 to 20% daily
drugs.notes: Peaks 4 to 6 hours after injection, matching a morning prednisolone dose.

drugs.name: Rapid-acting analogue or regular insulin (prandial)
drugs.dose: Half the TDD split across three meals SC; hold if the meal is not eaten
drugs.notes: Regular insulin 30 minutes before meals; analogues just before meals.

drugs.name: Correction insulin
drugs.dose: Low, medium or high scale for TDD below 40, 40 to 80, or above 80 units/day, starting at 140 to 150 mg/dL
drugs.notes: Before meals, or rapid-acting every 4 hours or regular every 6 hours if not eating.

drugs.name: Regular insulin IV infusion (ICU)
drugs.dose: Per validated protocol for glucose 180 mg/dL or more, target 140 to 180 mg/dL
drugs.notes: Glucose checks every 30 minutes to 2 hours.

drugs.name: Gliclazide (steroid-induced, mild)
drugs.dose: 40 mg orally each morning, titrated daily to a maximum of 240 mg in the morning (320 mg/day total)
drugs.notes: Reduce with steroid taper; hypoglycaemia risk in CKD and older adults.

drugs.name: Linagliptin
drugs.notes: Option with correction insulin for mild hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes; no renal dose adjustment.
